pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 7–9 years

- **Topic:** Inside a Volcano — magma is hot melted rock underground, lava is the SAME material once it reaches the surface, and a volcano has a magma chamber, vent and crater.

- **Standards — UK (KS2, mixed placement):** In England, volcanoes are taught in KS2 **Geography** (physical geography: "describe and understand key aspects of physical geography, including… volcanoes and earthquakes"), NOT in KS2 science. The nearest KS2 science hook is Y3 **Rocks** (igneous rock forms when lava/magma cools). Earth's internal structure and rock formation are formally DfE **KS3 Chemistry — Earth and atmosphere** ("the structure of the Earth"; "the rock cycle and the formation of igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks"). So this topic runs ahead of the UK science sequence and should be framed via Geography + Y3 Rocks.

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** No dedicated elementary PE for volcano anatomy. Volcanoes appear in **4-ESS2-2** ("[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-ESS2-2]"; clarification names volcanoes) and **2-ESS1-1** (Earth events, some quick like eruptions). Molten-rock/interior mechanism is not assessed until MS-ESS2. State-standard tier: DEFERRED.

- **Operational details:** Build on 'What Is a Volcano' (5–7) and 'Earth's Layers'. Anchor on ONE cutaway cross-section labelled magma chamber → vent → crater, and trace the path molten rock takes upward. The load-bearing idea is a NAMING-by-LOCATION rule: identical molten rock is called *magma* below ground and *lava* above it. Keep it concrete — a hidden interior made visible by a model.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete/observational, model-based). Children reason about an unseeable interior through a cutaway model; expect them to conflate magma and lava as different substances, and to picture the vent as bottomless. Success = correctly label the three parts and state that magma and lava are the same rock named by where it is.
bestPractices: Anchor everything on a single labelled CUTAWAY cross-section so the hidden interior becomes concrete and visible; introduce magma chamber, vent and crater on that one image before adding motion.

Teach the magma/lava distinction as a location rule, not two materials: 'same hot melted rock — magma underground, lava once it's out'. Say the sentence, then show one blob crossing the surface and being re-labelled.
Trace the eruption as a journey (chamber → up the vent → out of the crater) so parts are learned in causal order rather than as isolated labels.
Reinforce that this melted rock is astonishingly hot (hot enough to glow and melt solid rock), linking back to Earth's hot interior from 'Earth's Layers'.
Use the classic bicarbonate/vinegar or shaken-bottle model only as an analogy for the UPWARD PUSH, and explicitly flag its limits (it is not real rock, not real heat).
keyRepresentations: Labelled volcano cross-section (magma chamber, vent, crater) — the canonical teaching diagram
A single tracked blob of glowing molten rock travelling up the vent, re-labelled magma→lava at the crater rim
Colour/temperature cue: deep orange-white glowing rock underground cooling to dark grey rock once erupted
Cutaway 'X-ray view' of a mountain revealing the plumbing hidden inside
commonMisconceptions: Magma and lava are different substances (they are the same melted rock; the name changes at the surface).
Lava is fire, or the volcano is 'on fire' inside (it is glowing hot molten ROCK, not flame).
The vent is a bottomless hole straight to the Earth's core (it connects to a magma chamber, not the core).
A volcano is always a tall cone with a neat hole on top (shape varies; the crater is the surface opening).
The inside is hollow like a chimney (it is filled rock plumbing — chamber and vent — not an empty tube).

learn.summary: For ages 7–9: teach the inside of a volcano through a single labelled cutaway cross-section. Learners name the three parts (magma chamber, vent, crater), trace the path molten rock takes upward during an eruption, and grasp the load-bearing idea that magma and lava are the SAME hot melted rock — named by location (below ground vs above ground), not two different materials. Anchor on one image and one tracked blob of glowing rock whose NAME flips instantly as it crosses the surface, while its colour only cools gradually as the lava flows away.

activities.title: Follow one glowing blob up the volcano
feedback: If a learner says magma and lava are different materials: replay the single blob crossing the surface — 'It's the same melt, just renamed the instant it comes out at the surface.'
Lift-the-flap prompt at the crater: 'Is it magma or lava now?' → 'Lava — same rock, new name because it's outside.'
If a learner thinks lava is cold or dark the moment it erupts: 'Fresh lava is still glowing hot like the magma — it only cools and turns dark grey slowly as it flows away and loses heat.'
If a learner pictures the chamber as a hollow cave or underground lake: 'It's molten rock held within and among hot solid rock, not an empty cavern of pure liquid.'

If a learner traces the magma down to the Earth's core: 'Magma forms when rock melts deep underground, mostly in the upper mantle, and then collects in a magma chamber in the crust — not at the centre of the Earth.'
Reinforce that this melted rock is astonishingly hot — hot enough to glow and to melt solid rock — linking back to Earth's hot interior.
activities.rationale: The central insight is a CHANGE that is best watched rather than stated: driving pressure and following one re-labelled blob makes 'same rock, new name' concrete at a single visible moment. The floating label switch is instant (location rule) while live recolouring from orange-white to dark grey happens gradually as the lava flows — keeping the two timings distinct avoids suggesting lava cools the moment it erupts. These are optional interaction examples that make the naming-by-location mechanism observable, proposed as one effective way to surface the common magma-vs-lava confusion, not as the only way to teach it.
sourceClaims: Magma is molten rock below the surface; lava is the same molten rock once it erupts; volcanoes have a magma chamber, vent and crater.
learnerActions: Study a single labelled cutaway cross-section of a volcano, identifying the magma chamber, vent and crater on that one image before anything moves.
Build up pressure in the magma chamber and then release it, following ONE highlighted blob of glowing melted rock as it pushes up from the chamber, through the vent, and out of the crater.

Watch and say aloud what happens as the blob reaches the surface: the instant it comes out of the top of the vent into the open air (in the crater) its NAME changes from 'magma' to 'lava'. This is just a location rule, and the rock is still the same glowing-hot melt. Then watch the lava flow away from the vent and only GRADUALLY cool and darken, from glowing orange-white toward dark grey rock. It is the same stuff throughout: a new name straight away and a cooler colour later.
Tap each part (chamber, vent, crater) to pin its name as the blob passes it, so the anatomy is learned in the causal order of the eruption journey.
activities.intendedInsight: Magma and lava are one and the same melted rock; the name depends only on WHERE it is (underground = magma, surface = lava), and it changes the instant the rock crosses the surface. Freshly erupted lava is still glowing hot — it only cools and darkens over time. A volcano's interior is filled rock plumbing — a magma chamber connected by a vent to a crater opening — not a hollow tube or a path to the Earth's core.

activities.title: Label and reveal the cross-section
feedback: For the crater flap: 'Lava — same rock, new name because it's outside.'
If a learner expects a tall neat cone every time: 'Volcano shapes vary; the crater is simply the surface opening, wherever it is.'
If the interior is imagined as hollow like a chimney: zoom in to show it is filled rock plumbing, not an empty tube.
activities.rationale: Much of this topic is fixed labelling (chamber, vent, crater) that suits tap-to-reveal and drill-down zoom. A static labelled image supports naming and fact recall well; it does not by itself enact the magma→lava relabel, so pair it with the dynamic blob activity for the change insight. This is a complementary scaffold, not a claim that a static image cannot teach the distinction.
sourceClaims: Magma is molten rock below the surface; lava is the same molten rock once it erupts; volcanoes have a magma chamber, vent and crater.
learnerActions: On a static labelled cross-section, tap the magma chamber, vent and crater to reveal a short fact card for each.
Use a drill-down zoom into the magma chamber to see glowing melted rock held among hot rock (not an empty cave).
Answer a lift-the-flap at the crater rim: 'Is it magma or lava now, and why?'
activities.intendedInsight: The volcano's hidden interior can be made visible and named: chamber, vent, crater — with the magma chamber being molten rock within rock, and the crater being the surface opening.

activities.title: Consolidate the parts and the naming rule
feedback: Correct the path order if muddled: molten rock rises from the chamber, up the vent, and out of the crater.
If a learner picks a wrong name for above-ground rock: prompt them to state WHERE it is, then name it ('surface = lava').
activities.rationale: Recall and matching tasks consolidate labels and the magma-vs-lava rule after the concept is met. This format checks recall rather than delivering the moment of insight, so it should follow — not replace — the dynamic and reveal activities.
learnerActions: Drag labels onto a blank cross-section to place the magma chamber, vent and crater correctly.
Sequence the eruption journey in order: chamber → vent → crater.
Answer: 'The melted rock is now above ground — what do we call it?' and explain the reason in one sentence.
activities.intendedInsight: Learners can independently recall the anatomy and state the naming-by-location rule in their own words.

activities.title: Pressure-push model as a flagged analogy
feedback: Prompt the limit aloud: 'This shows the upward push, but it is not real rock and not real heat — real magma glows because it is extremely hot.'
activities.rationale: A physical push-model makes the 'why it comes up' intuition concrete, provided its limits are flagged so learners do not transfer 'fizz/foam' to 'molten rock'.
learnerActions: Watch or run a classic bicarbonate/vinegar reaction or a shaken fizzy-bottle release to feel how built-up pressure pushes material UP and out.
State explicitly how this model is and is NOT like a real volcano.
activities.intendedInsight: An eruption is driven by an upward push from built-up pressure — but the analogy is limited: the fizz is not real molten rock and not real heat.

constraints: Keep everything anchored on ONE labelled cutaway cross-section before adding motion, so the hidden interior stays concrete and visible.
Teach magma/lava as a location rule, not two substances: say 'same hot melted rock — magma underground, lava once it's out', then show one blob crossing the surface and being re-labelled.

Treat the name change as instant at the surface but the colour change as gradual: fresh lava is still glowing hot and only cools and darkens to dark grey over time as it flows away — do not depict lava turning cold/dark the moment it erupts.
Introduce parts in causal order along the eruption journey (chamber → vent → crater), not as an isolated label list.
The bicarbonate/vinegar or shaken-bottle demonstration is only an analogy for the upward push; explicitly flag that it is not real rock and not real heat.
Drag-label, matching and multiple-choice tasks check recall only; they do not by themselves elicit the moment of insight that magma and lava are the same rock.

Interaction examples (pressure control, live recolouring, floating label switch, tap-to-pin, drill-down zoom) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete — not mandatory mechanisms or specific products.

This runs ahead of the UK KS2 science sequence: frame via KS2 Geography (physical geography: volcanoes/earthquakes) plus Y3 Rocks; Earth's internal structure and the rock cycle are formally KS3 Chemistry. In the US it is not an elementary focus for interior mechanism (deferred to MS-ESS2); volcanoes appear in 4-ESS2-2 and 2-ESS1-1 at map/event level.

Correct lingering misconceptions explicitly: lava is glowing hot molten ROCK, not fire/flame; the vent connects to a magma chamber, not straight to the core; the interior is filled rock plumbing, not a hollow chimney.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the four legacy sources are marked verified:false (DfE KS2 Geography placement; USGS magma-vs-lava/anatomy). The core factual claim (magma below, lava above, chamber/vent/crater) is standard but carries an unverified flag in the row.

The legacy '3D adds nothing at this age' and 'a static picture cannot enact the relabel / only this delivers the insight' framings are catalog fit judgements, not established efficacy findings; they are softened to scoped affordance/limit statements. A rotatable sliceable 3D model is retained as an optional spatial extension, not dismissed.

The reteach line 'magma forms in a chamber in the crust/upper mantle' is an age-appropriate simplification (magma generally originates in the mantle and collects in a crustal chamber); accurate enough for 7–9 and consistent with the source row, but a simplification to note.

The dynamic activity correctly separates the two timings: the NAME flips instantly at the surface (a location rule) while the lava stays glowing hot and only cools and darkens gradually as it flows away — this avoids wrongly depicting erupted lava as cold or dark. No arithmetic or force/motion content to audit here.
Independent re-review confirmed no lingering occurrence depicts lava cooling/darkening at the instant of eruption across summary, insights, actions, feedback or constraints.

probeDeeper: If we could follow one drop of the melted rock from underground to pouring out the top, when would its name change from magma to lava?
Point to the magma chamber, the vent, and the crater on this diagram.
Is the magma chamber a big empty cave, or something else?
Where does the magma form — near the top, or deep down at the very centre of the Earth?
assess.correctAnswer: They're the SAME melted rock — the name just changes depending on where it is. Underground it's called magma; once it erupts out onto the surface it becomes lava. It travels up from the magma chamber, through the vent, and out of the crater.

errorPatterns.pattern: Magma and lava are two different materials
errorPatterns.nextMove: Follow one blob up the vent — it's the same melt, renamed the instant it crosses the surface.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says they're made of different things, not the same rock.

errorPatterns.pattern: The magma chamber is a big hollow cave full of liquid, like an underground lake
errorPatterns.nextMove: It's molten rock held within and among hot rock, not an empty cave.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Describes a hollow cavern of pure liquid rock.

errorPatterns.pattern: The lava comes all the way up from the Earth's molten centre / core
errorPatterns.nextMove: Magma forms in a chamber in the crust/upper mantle, not at the centre of the Earth.
errorPatterns.distractor: The lava comes all the way up from the centre of the Earth.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Traces the magma down to the core.

responseLevels.gap: Thinks magma and lava are different materials; can't trace the path to the surface.
responseLevels.full: Explains magma and lava are the same melted rock renamed by location (underground vs surface) and traces the path chamber → vent → crater.
responseLevels.partial: Labels the parts and uses both words but still treats magma and lava as different substances, or muddles the path.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A child says the hot melted rock inside a volcano is called 'magma', and the stuff that pours out of the top is a totally different thing called 'lava'. Are magma and lava two different materials, or the same thing? Explain your answer.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child can label the parts (chamber, vent, crater) and use both words yet think magma and lava are different substances. Asking whether they're the same forces the location-not-material insight; a child holding the misconception insists they're different stuffs.
